Jaguars vs Ravens prediction, pick, spread and over/under for Thursday night in Week 9: my pick is Baltimore +9.5 and the Over 42, with a final of Jaguars 25, Ravens 21. Baltimore spends Thursday evening at MICA's Pinkard Gallery, where Globe Posters for the People opens at 5 p.m. to honor the city's loudest print shop, and the Ravens need that kind of volume with Lamar Jackson gone and a rookie in his place.

Kickoff is 8:15 p.m. Eastern at M&T Bank Stadium. The consensus sits at Jacksonville −9.5 with the over/under at 42 as of Nov 3, 12:15 p.m. ET. The spread opened at −9 and the over/under at 42.5, so this market has barely moved.

Start with the quarterback, because everything else follows. Jackson hurt his right thumb on his first snap in Buffalo, a 36-10 loss, and he is headed for injured reserve. Tyler Huntley came in, hurt his toe, and is out Thursday and a candidate for IR too. That leaves Joe Fagnano, the undrafted rookie out of Connecticut, who went 10-of-21 for 91 yards with an interception in relief and was limited in Monday's walk-through with an ankle injury. Minter named Fagnano the starter Tuesday, and he practiced in a brace on that ankle. That's a real drop, and I'm pricing it as one.

The number already did most of that work, though. Nine and a half is a big ask for a road team on four days' rest after a 681-mile trip. The Formula: Net grades Baltimore Ravens −4.0, Jacksonville Jaguars 0.7 (nflverse play-by-play, Nov 3, 2026). Knock Baltimore down hard for the quarterback mess and you still land short of 9.5.

The ground game is where Baltimore hangs around. The Ravens run for 4.8 yards a carry, and Minter will want to keep whoever plays quarterback out of long downs. Jacksonville's run defense allows just 3.4, so this won't be easy, but a steady run game means a short game and a shorter clock. Kyle Hamilton and Roquan Smith give Baltimore enough on defense to keep Trevor Lawrence honest in the fourth quarter.

The Over looks wrong at first glance with a backup at quarterback, which is exactly why the over/under sits as low as 42. Baltimore has allowed 203 points in eight games. Jacksonville has scored 196 in seven. Every short field off a Baltimore mistake becomes Jacksonville points, and the Ravens have 179 points this season to prove they can answer. Jaguars 25, Ravens 21 is 46, four clear of the number.

The room moved after the quarterback news. Next Man Up has Jaguars 26, Ravens 19, a 45-point game, and it no longer likes the Ravens with the points. All four with a pick like the Over. Follow The Money has no pick on either one because the consensus has moved only half a point each way.

Ivy Corcoran will tell you Jacksonville is 5-2 and Baltimore is 4-4, and she's right. Owen Pratt will tell you Baltimore wins ugly or not at all. I'll split the difference: the Jaguars win, and the poster doesn't get printed for a blowout.

games.fanatic_story:
Jacksonville Jaguars vs Baltimore Ravens in Week 9 lands on a Thursday night when Baltimore is literally hanging DayGlo on the walls: MICA's Pinkard Gallery on Mount Royal Avenue opens Globe Posters for the People at 5 p.m., a show built around the old Baltimore print shop whose screaming fluorescent show posters sold concerts and fight nights to this whole town. Owen Pratt will be standing in that gallery about three hours before the 8:15 kickoff, looking for a poster loud enough to announce whoever plays quarterback, while Ivy Corcoran, up from Duval with her standings sheet folded in her jacket, asks him why he's shopping for art on the worst week of his football life.

Here's the worst week. Lamar Jackson hurt his right thumb on Baltimore's very first offensive snap in Orchard Park on Sunday, a 36-10 loss, and is headed for injured reserve. Tyler Huntley came in, hurt his toe, has already been ruled out for Thursday and is a candidate to go to IR. That leaves Joe Fagnano, the undrafted kid out of Connecticut, who finished the loss in Buffalo, is nursing an ankle injury and was limited in Monday's walk-through. On Tuesday Jesse Minter made it official: Fagnano starts Thursday. Baltimore had three different quarterbacks throw before halftime, something no NFL team had done since the Cowboys nine seasons ago.

Owen: Globe knew how to sell a night. Big block letters, fluorescent ink, one night only. I want one that says BALTIMORE in letters you can read from the upper deck.

Ivy: Put the record on it too. Baltimore 4-4, Jacksonville 5-2. That's the only print I need.

That's Ivy in one sentence. She doesn't argue with feelings, she argues with the standings, and right now the standings say Jacksonville sits on top of the AFC South. The Jaguars have scored 196 points and allowed 111 in seven games. Baltimore has scored 179 and allowed 203 in eight, and it is 1-2 at home.

Owen grew up reading box scores from the bottom up. Sacks, takeaways, then whoever was throwing. In his house, defense signs the checks, and he has two Lombardi Trophies to wave around when anybody doubts it. Super Bowl XXXV was a Ray Lewis production with Trent Dilfer handing off. A rookie quarterback in a jam is not the end of the world to Owen. It's the plan.

Owen: Minter isn't going to ask a backup to win it. He's going to keep handing it off until the clock starts begging, and he's going to let Kyle Hamilton and Roquan Smith turn Thursday night into a fistfight.

Ivy: Your front has been run through all fall. Two hundred and three, Owen. I didn't write that number on the poster. Your defense did.

He has no comeback for that, so he goes after the ground game, where Baltimore actually has a case. The Ravens run for 4.8 yards a carry. Jacksonville's defense, though, gives up only 3.4, one of the meanest run fronts in the league, and the Jaguars run for 4.6 against a Baltimore defense that allows 3.8. Thursday becomes a shoving match at the point of attack, and Ivy likes her side of that shove.

Ivy also gave something up for this trip. Back home, JJ Grey & Mofro are playing the Jax Amphitheater at the Greater Jacksonville Agricultural Fair on Thursday night, out at the fair's new grounds on Normandy Boulevard. She traded swamp funk and a fried-everything midway for a short week, a cold parking lot on Russell Street and a quarterback room held together with tape.

Owen: You'll be back for the fair. It runs eleven days. My season might not.

Ivy: That's the first true thing you've said all night.

Here's how it goes. Baltimore gets its carries, whoever plays quarterback makes a couple of throws that make the stadium stand up, and Hamilton and Smith keep it ugly enough that Owen still likes his chances in the fourth quarter. Then Trevor Lawrence finds one more drive than Baltimore can answer, and the Jaguars leave town with a road win and Ivy's standings sheet still folded neatly in her jacket.

Owen buys the poster anyway. He says it'll look better next January.

My call: Jaguars 25, Ravens 21.

Cincinnati Bengals vs Atlanta Falcons in Week 9 goes to Madrid, and the first thing both fan bases will see in town is a ring from every Super Bowl ever played, lined up in a glass case inside the NFL House at the Casa de las Alhajas on Plaza de San Martín. Laura Kessel and Russ Amundsen walked in together on Friday, found the Lombardi Trophy, counted every ring from the first one forward, and came up empty for both of their teams.

Laura: Not one. We came four thousand miles to look at other people's jewelry.

Russ: Speak for yourself. I've looked at other people's jewelry my whole life. I'm a Falcons fan.

The building makes it worse. The Casa de las Alhajas was a nineteenth-century pawn-and-savings bank, a place where people in Madrid brought their valuables in and hoped to get them back someday. Russ stood beneath that ceiling and thought about February in Houston and a lead he still won't say out loud. Laura thought about three Super Bowl trips and three long flights home. They agreed not to talk about it, which lasted roughly eleven seconds.

Then it was down to Plaza de España, where the league set up flag football for kids and a Bengals Menina, one of those big painted Meninas statues Madrid puts around the city, dressed in tiger stripes. Dallas Cowboys vs Indianapolis Colts in Week 9 arrives the same weekend the Indianapolis Ballet stages its first-ever company Cinderella at Clowes Hall with the Indianapolis Symphony Orchestra in the pit, and Lou Ferraro has decided that's not a coincidence. A 2-6 team, a famous visitor rolling up in a shiny coach, and a clock everybody's watching. Cole Garrison, down from Dallas with a carry-on full of team gear, points out that in this version the Colts are the ones sweeping up.

Lou: Cinderella was nobody at the ball until she wasn't. That's all I'm saying.

Cole: Cinderella had a fairy godmother. You've got Daniel Jones.

That stings, because it's true. Jones threw two interceptions in the forty-two to seven beating at Jacksonville last week and got pulled late for Anthony Richardson, and on Monday Shane Steichen said Jones keeps the job against Dallas. Lou took that news the way he takes everything: with a history lesson.

Lou measures every Colts season against the whole family tree, not just the Indianapolis branch. He'll start with Johnny Unitas and the Baltimore years, walk through the Mayflower trucks leaving in the snow in the spring of nineteen eighty-four, and land on Peyton Manning and the Lombardi in Miami before you can stop him. Continuity is his religion. Teams that keep their quarterback, keep their coach and keep their nerve win in the end. Teams that panic in November stay 2-6.

Lou: Steichen didn't blink. I respect that. Panic is how you end up shopping for a quarterback every March.

Cole lets that one go, because Cole's whole life is the gap between the Dallas brand and the Dallas results. He can tell you exactly how many people in Mexico, Japan and Ohio own a Cowboys hoodie, and he can tell you how many of those people have seen Dallas reach a conference title game since the Aikman years. The first number is enormous. The second one isn't.

Last Sunday was the brand-versus-results problem in one afternoon. Dallas led Arizona by 14 in the fourth quarter and lost it, with Gardner Minshew bringing the Cardinals all the way back. Cole spent the flight to Indianapolis staring at the seatback in front of him. Dallas is 3-5 now, with 219 points scored and 213 allowed, which means the offense shows up every week and the defense keeps handing it back.

Cole: Dak Prescott is fine. CeeDee Lamb is fine. George Pickens is fine. We scored plenty. We just keep giving it away in the fourth quarter like it's a door prize.

Lou: In Indy we'd call that a Sunday.

Here is where Lou actually has something. Neither defense stops the run. Dallas gives up 5.2 yards a carry, and Indianapolis gives up 5.2 too. The Colts run for 4.2 and the Cowboys run for only 3.8, so whichever back gets loose first sets the tone. Lou wants the Colts to stop asking Jones to win it with his arm and just keep handing it off into a defense that hasn't proven it can tackle.

The Colts are 1-2 at Lucas Oil and have scored 161 points in eight games, which Lou admits is nowhere near the Manning years. He also notes that 161 points scored and 222 allowed still make for a team that's been in more fights than its record says. Cole notes that it's still 2-6.

The weekend around the game helps Lou's mood. Christmas Nights of Lights opens Friday at the State Fairgrounds, and Sunday is the last day of Heroes from the Heartland at the Indiana State Museum, the exhibit honoring Hoosier veterans, which Lou plans to walk through with his grandson before kickoff. Cole asked if they make the Cowboys' fans pay extra for parking. Lou said only when they lose.

For one Sunday afternoon, Lucas Oil gets to be the ballroom. Lou thinks Jones finally keeps the ball in his own hands for four quarters and the Colts' run game punishes a defense that blew a 14-point lead a week ago. Cole thinks the clock strikes twelve on Indy the way it always does.

Lou says this time the slipper fits.

My call: Colts 27, Cowboys 24.

Mike thinks his guys hang around long enough to make everybody nervous.

Chet's ledger closes the same way every season: wins first, style points never.

Detroit Lions vs Miami Dolphins in Week 9 shares a Sunday with the NASCAR Cup Series championship at Homestead-Miami Speedway, four hundred miles for the title, green flag at 3 p.m., about two hours after kickoff at Hard Rock Stadium. Martin Sorensen flew down from Detroit for both, because a man from the Motor City doesn't get many chances to watch a championship race and a Lions road win on the same afternoon. Carla Ruiz, who has lived through more Dolphins rebuilds than she can count, asked him to choose one.

Martin: I can do both. Kickoff at one, checkered flag by dinner. That's called planning.

Carla: That's called traffic on the Turnpike. You'll see the last ten laps on your phone.

Martin lives on a clock. He's a window-urgency guy, and the window in Detroit is wide open right now. Jared Goff, Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jahmyr Gibbs, Aidan Hutchinson, a roster built to win now, and Martin wakes up every day afraid that now ends tomorrow. The Lions are 5-2 and have won three straight, the last one an emotional win against Minnesota, and Martin is treating every remaining Sunday like a lap he can't get back.

Martin: You don't waste a car like this one. You don't park it in the garage and admire it. You run it until the tires come off.

Carla: That's a nice speech for a team that's 1-2 on the road.

She's not wrong, and Martin knows it. Detroit is 4-0 at Ford Field and 1-2 everywhere else. The Lions have scored 203 points and allowed 180, which tells you the defense has been bending all fall. The local paper in Michigan called this team injury-riddled this week, and Martin read that headline three times on the plane.

Carla is the opposite kind of fan. She doesn't panic about windows, she studies blueprints. Miami is 1-6 and 0-3 at home, and she'll tell you that's what a teardown looks like from the inside. A first-year head coach in Jeff Hafley, who ran the defense in Green Bay, and a quarterback in Malik Willis who started the last game. Carla isn't asking for a playoff run. She's asking for evidence that the new plan works, and lately she's gotten some.

Carla: Our last four games were all one-score games. You know what a rebuilding team looks like when it's going nowhere? It gets blown out. We aren't getting blown out.

Martin: You're 1-6.

Carla: We're 1-6 and close. There's a difference, and Hafley's defense is the difference.

Miami runs it. Ollie Gordon II has been carrying the load, and the Dolphins get 4.6 yards a carry against a Detroit defense that gives up 4.3. Detroit runs for 4.7 against a Miami defense that allows 4.2, and Gibbs is the kind of back who turns half a yard of daylight into a long afternoon for a defense. That's Martin's whole plan: give it to Gibbs, let Goff work off it, and get out of town.

There's some history pushing Martin along, too. Detroit has won its last two trips to Miami. Carla points out the Dolphins still lead the all-time series, and she says it like a woman who has been waiting all season to win an argument.

Then there's the heat. Early November in South Florida still feels like summer to a guy whose phone is showing Detroit weather. Martin brought one jacket and won't need it.

Carla's ask for Sunday is simple: keep it close, keep Willis upright, and make Detroit earn every yard. Martin's ask is louder. He wants the Lions to put this one away early so he can make it down to Homestead for the finish. Carla told him the Dolphins' rebuild doesn't care about his race schedule.

Somebody wins a championship in Homestead on Sunday evening. Martin just wants the Lions to win something smaller first, on the way to something bigger in January.

My call: Lions 27, Dolphins 22.

The Oak Street Po-Boy Festival opens at 10 a.m. with about 50 vendors stretched from South Carrollton Avenue to Eagle Street, and Andre intends to hit as many of them as he can before he heads downtown.

Frank Haller got to town a day early and went to Beignet Fest in City Park. He came back with powdered sugar caked on his Browns jacket and a confession.

Frank: "They sold me a crab rangoon beignet. Crab. In a doughnut. I've been a Browns fan my whole life, and I thought I'd seen every bad idea a person can have."

Andre: "And?"

Frank: "I had two."

That's Frank. He's the guy in every Cleveland section who wants to talk about 1946 before you've found your seat. His motto is "Look before 1965," and he means it. Four AAFC titles from 1946 to 1949. NFL championships in 1950, 1954, 1955 and 1964. He'll put Otto Graham up against any quarterback from any era, and he'll remind you Brian Sipe was the 1980 MVP before you can change the subject.

Andre: "Every time you say 1964, somebody in this city gets a headache."

Frank: "You've got one Lombardi Trophy."

Andre: "One is plenty when you built it yourself. Development is a timeline, Frank. Decades of paper bags, then Super Bowl XLIV and Tracy Porter taking that interception back for the touchdown that sealed it. We grew into it."

Andre is the Saints fan who grades a franchise by what it grows at home. Rickey Jackson. Willie Roaf. Morten Andersen. He can walk you through the draft classes that built the 2009 team and tell you which scout deserves a statue.

This year he's watching a slow build turn into a slow headache. The Saints are 2-5, and they're 0-3 in their own building. Both wins came on the road.

Andre: "Oh and three in the Dome. My mother called and asked if the team forgot the address."

Frank: "You had a week off to fix it."

Andre: "We had a week off to stew in it. Kellen Moore got extra time with Shough. Brandon Staley got extra time to draw up something mean for your guy. Rested team, home crowd, nothing left to lose. That's a dangerous animal."

Frank isn't as calm as the beignets suggest. Cleveland is 3-0 at home and 2-3 on the road, and this is a second straight trip after Pittsburgh. Worse, the Browns have given up more points than they've scored. Frank knows it. He just refuses to say it out loud inside the Dome.

Andre: "You win the close ones until you don't."

Frank: "Look before 1965, Andre. We were winning close ones when your team was a rumor."

Andre: "We were born in 1967. You're telling me to look at a time before we existed."

Frank: "Exactly. You weren't around to stop us."

Here's how Sunday plays out. Andre gets his po-boys and makes kickoff with a minute to spare. Frank spends the fourth quarter on his feet, yelling about Paul Brown to people who never asked. Cleveland keeps it tight the whole way, because that's who this team is. The Saints finally win one in their own building, and it takes every last snap.

Philadelphia doesn't have to be good on Sunday. It has to be stubborn for three hours.

Start with the quarterbacks, because this one's strange. In each team's last game, the man under center wasn't the guy who's started most of the season. J.J. McCarthy played for New York instead of Jameis Winston, and Tanner McKee played for Philadelphia instead of Jalen Hurts. games.fanatic_story:
New York Giants vs Philadelphia Eagles, Week 9, Sunday at 1 p.m. ET on Fox at Lincoln Financial Field. The Giants show up 4-2-1 and fresh off a bye. The Eagles are 2-6 and sick of hearing about it. Ray Donnelly spent Saturday morning at the Rocky Steps Challenge at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, where the goal is 72 steps in less than 12 seconds.

Ray: "Eleven point something. I'm telling everybody eleven point something."

Leon: "Who timed it?"

Ray: "A guy."

Leon Drobny rode down from North Jersey and has been in a sour mood since he crossed the bridge. Not because of the Eagles. Because of the Giants. Leon's whole creed is "Respect the upset." He was raised on 17-14, the night the Giants wrecked New England's perfect season in Super Bowl XLII. He has the 21-17 from Super Bowl XLVI framed in his hallway. He loves his team most when nobody outside the building gives them a chance.

Leon: "Now everybody expects us to win this thing. I hate it. I don't know what to do with my hands."

Ray: "Put 'em in your pockets. It's November in Philly."

Ray judges everything by the guards. Give him two guys who can pull and a center who can talk and he'll show you a parade. He was on Broad Street after Super Bowl LIX, when the Eagles beat Kansas City 40-22, and he'll describe it to you whether you ask or not.

Ray: "Watch the guards, Leon. Everything starts there. This year it's been a mess, and I'm not hiding from it."

Leon: "You've given up 202 points."

Ray: "I can count, thank you."

Both of them are carrying the same strange worry into Sunday. In each team's last game, the quarterback wasn't the guy who started most of the year. J.J. McCarthy took the snaps for the Giants instead of Jameis Winston. Tanner McKee went for Philadelphia instead of Jalen Hurts. The Week 9 injury report isn't out, and neither of these two is going to pretend he knows more than he does.

Leon: "Whoever it is, John Harbaugh will have him ready. The man won a Super Bowl in Baltimore."

Ray: "Sirianni won one here two seasons ago, and Vic Fangio's still running our defense. I'll take my chances with that."

Then it turns into a history fight, because it always does with these two.

Leon: "Four championships before the Super Bowl even existed. 1927, 1934, 1938, 1956. Then 1986, 1990, 2007 and 2011. Go ahead, count yours."

Ray: "Bednarik. Chuck Bednarik played both ways and hit like a car wreck. Steve Van Buren. Reggie White. 1948, 1949, 1960. And Super Bowl LII, when Nick Foles caught a touchdown on fourth down and the whole city lost its mind."

Leon: "We beat an undefeated team. In the Super Bowl. Nobody else can say that."

Ray: "We beat Brady with a backup quarterback and a trick play the whole city still runs in the backyard."

Leon: "Fine. That one was good."

Ray: "Write it down. A Giants fan said something nice."

Here's how it plays. The Giants grind out a few long drives, the Eagles stay right in their face, and the Linc spends the fourth quarter at full volume. Leon gets his win, and he'll be miserable about how close it was, which is the most Giants thing possible. Ray walks out insisting the guards were better, and for once the tape will back him up.

My call: Giants 22, Eagles 21.

An hour before kickoff, the fourth annual National Veterans Parade steps off on Constitution Avenue, running from the National Archives toward the White House. It's a big Sunday in the region, and the Commanders need their own crowd loud.

The case for Los Angeles is real. The Rams are 4-4, but they've scored 194 and allowed 168, and they're 2-1 on the road. The Formula and In The Trenches both have Rams 27, Commanders 20, and both lay the 5.5. Los Angeles gains 5.0 yards a carry. Washington allows 4.0. Something gives.

Washington runs for 4.8 a carry against a Rams defense allowing 4.0, and Daniels gives Dan Quinn a way to keep the chains going when a drive stalls. Los Angeles is flying 2311 miles east for a game that starts at 10 a.m. on its body clock. Both teams are on 7 days of rest, so the trip is the only scheduling difference.

My card is Washington Commanders 21, Los Angeles Rams 26. A five-point Rams win keeps Washington Commanders +5.5 alive by the hook. I won't pretend that's comfortable. It's the honest read. The total comes out at 47, a half-point under 47.5. Washington has allowed 182 in seven games and Los Angeles 168 in eight, but I see a game played on the ground, which eats clock and keeps both teams stuck in the 20s.

The room splits right down the middle on the side. The Formula and In The Trenches take the Rams −5.5, both at Rams 27, Commanders 20. Next Man Up and Letdown Watch take Washington +5.5, with Next Man Up at Rams 26, Commanders 22 and Letdown Watch at Rams 25, Commanders 21. Three cards are on the Under: The Formula, Letdown Watch and In The Trenches. Next Man Up is the lone Over. Follow The Money has no pick in this game.

Sean McVay will have a plan, and he has Kliff Kingsbury, Washington's old offensive coordinator, sitting next to him. That's a real wrinkle. Quinn has seen plenty of McVay, though, and his team is a different animal at home. I want the points and a game that grinds.

Denver Broncos vs Carolina Panthers, Week 9, Sunday at 1 p.m. ET at Bank of America Stadium. Bo Nix brings a 6-2 Denver team to Charlotte. Bryce Young and the 3-4 Panthers have had 10 days to get ready. Mitch Kovac has had ten days to get angry.

Mitch: "Super Bowl 50. Don't."

Ruth: "I didn't say a word."

Mitch: "You're wearing the Von Miller jersey. You said it with your shirt."

Ruth Calder came in from Denver with an Elway story for every situation. Her question about any quarterback is "Where's he in the arc?" Elway lost three Super Bowls before he won two, XXXII and XXXIII, and Ruth figures every Broncos quarterback since has been somewhere on that same road. Then came 24-10 in Super Bowl 50, February 2016. She keeps Terrell Davis, Champ Bailey and Floyd Little in the conversation the way some people keep family photos in their wallet.

Ruth: "Nix is early in the arc. Second-year guys learn, third-year guys win. This is his third year. Do the math."

Mitch: "Bryce is in his fourth. Do that math."

Mitch doesn't care about arcs. He cares about the depth chart. "Show me the depth chart" is how he answers every question, including what's for lunch. He grew up on Sam Mills, Julius Peppers and Luke Kuechly, and he still leaves the room when someone brings up Super Bowl XXXVIII. He studies the two-deep like it's a tax return and he's getting audited.

Ruth spent Saturday up in Huntersville at the Carolina Renaissance Festival, because she says anybody who survived the Elway years can handle a day around people in armor. Mitch skipped it. He spent Saturday walking past the Carolinas Veterans Day Festival at Romare Bearden Park and then sat home watching tape. The Ally Tipoff is uptown at the Spectrum Center on Sunday afternoon, South Carolina against North Carolina and NC State against Kentucky in women's college basketball, so Charlotte gets a full day of yelling no matter what happens at the stadium.

Then they get into the actual teams, which is where it gets loud.

Mitch: "We've scored 178. You've scored 172 in one more game. Whose offense is the scary one?"

Ruth: "The one that's 6-2."

Mitch: "We won the division last year."

Ruth: "So did we. And we've been perfect at home."

Mitch: "This isn't your home."

Ruth: "Fine. We're 2-2 away. I'll take Sean Payton's game plan against anybody's on the road. The man has a play for every situation, and three backups for every play."

Mitch: "Dave Canales has Ejiro Evero running our defense, and Evero coached in your building. He knows where you keep the spare keys."

That last one lands, and Ruth knows it. Both of them also know the ugly truth: these defenses give up points. Denver has allowed 165. Carolina has allowed 193. Neither of them expects a shutout, and both of them are already nervous about the fourth quarter.

Here's how it goes. Sunday stays tight into the final minutes. Young keeps Carolina right there, the stadium stays loud the whole way, and Mitch spends most of the second half on his feet screaming about tackling angles. But Nix makes the late throws a third-year quarterback is supposed to make, and Ruth gets to say the word "arc" about forty more times on the drive home.

My call: Broncos 24, Panthers 22.

Houston Texans vs Los Angeles Chargers, Week 9, Sunday at 4:05 p.m. ET at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood. C.J. Stroud against Justin Herbert. A 2-5 team against an 0-7 team. Marty Szabo has the tape cued up on a laptop in the parking lot, and he's not taking questions about the record.

Marty: "Roll the tape. Not the scoreboard. The tape."

Nate: "The tape says oh and seven, Marty."

Marty: "The tape says we played the Rams in our own stadium and it counted as a road game. That's not football. That's paperwork."

Marty is a Chargers lifer who goes back further than most people in Los Angeles realize this team does. He'll tell you about the 1963 AFL championship and Lance Alworth before you've parked. Ron Mix. Dan Fouts. The AFC title in the 1994 season. He keeps a running list of every bad bounce since the San Diego days, and it's long enough to need a table of contents.

Nate Coleman flew in from Houston with one rule: pressure tells the truth. Put a defender in a quarterback's face and Nate wants to know what happens next. He's been a Texans fan since the very first season in 2002, and his Hall of Fame list is short: Andre Johnson. He'll talk about Andre for an hour if you let him, and he won't let you leave.

Nate: "We're 0-4 at home and 2-1 on the road. I'm starting to think the problem is Houston."

Marty: "You want to switch? We've got road games at home. Best of both worlds."

The two of them have been friends since a Texans trip out here years ago, and the insults have only gotten sharper.

Nate: "We had the week off. DeMeco Ryans had two weeks to get the front ready. Stroud got a breather. Our guys are coming to hit people."

Marty: "Jim Harbaugh has been waiting all season for somebody to hit back. That man would coach a fistfight if they let him."

Nate: "You've scored 99 points in seven games."

Marty: "Quality points. Handcrafted."

Marty's real hope is the offense. Mike McDaniel is running it now, and Marty swears it looks better on film than it does on the scoreboard. Herbert still makes throws nobody else in the league tries. The problem is everything around those throws, and Marty knows it.

Marty: "Every week I watch the tape, and every week I see the play that should've changed it. One block. One catch. That's it."

Nate: "That's what every 0-7 guy says."

Marty: "And every 2-5 guy flies 1,375 miles to say it to my face."

Marty: "Roll the tape on Monday. We'll see who's telling the truth."

Green Bay Packers at New England Patriots is Jordan Love and Matt LaFleur against Drake Maye and Mike Vrabel, 4:25 p.m. Eastern on Fox at Gillette Stadium. It comes one day after Foxborough puts Rob Gronkowski into the Patriots Hall of Fame on Patriot Place Plaza, which is how Paul Lindgren ended up standing in a crowd of Patriots fans on Saturday, arms folded, waiting for somebody to bring up Green Bay.

Glen Tolliver brought him. Glen thought it would be educational.

Glen: Nine seasons. Three Super Bowls here. Eighty touchdowns, a team record. That's not a highlight tape, Paul. That's a stack of receipts.

Paul: Second-round choice out of Arizona. Forty-second overall. I always respect a guy half the league let walk past them. Now, while we're counting things.

Glen: Here it comes.

Paul: Thirteen championships in Green Bay. Eleven before the merger, and that includes Super Bowls I and II. Then XXXI and XLV. Every one of them gets its own page.

Glen: We have six Super Bowls. I keep them filed. None of them is going to block anybody Sunday afternoon.

That's Glen in one sentence. He treats titles like tax records, proof the work got done once and useless for this year's return. Paul is the other kind of stubborn. He doesn't care who had the best October. He cares who gets written down in February, and he has never once gotten misty about a regular-season award.

They walked the plaza while the Bass Pro crowd lined up for Santa's arrival at five. Paul asked who brings Santa to a football town in the first week of November. Glen said the same people who put a Hall of Fame next to a shopping center, and he meant it as a compliment.

Then they got to Sunday.

Both teams are 5-3. New England is 3-0 at Gillette and 2-3 away from it, and the Patriots went to Miami last Sunday and came home with a 24-19 win. Green Bay beat Carolina 27-19 last Thursday night, so the Packers have had ten days to heal up and study, and they're 2-2 on the road.

Paul: Ten days. We could have driven here.

Glen: You'd have stopped in every town to explain Super Bowl I.

Paul: Only the ones that asked.

The scoring tells you what kind of afternoon to expect. New England has put up 184 points and allowed 162. Green Bay has 171 and 164. Two teams that grind, not two teams that race.

Paul builds his case around Love and Tucker Kraft. A tight end who breaks tackles in November is worth more than a speech, and Christian Watson stretching the field is what opens the middle for him. On the back end, Xavier McKinney plays like he owns the deed.

Glen: Maye isn't chasing anybody's legend. He's trying to make the right throw on third down. Put A.J. Brown on one side and Hunter Henry in the middle, keep Rhamondre Stevenson behind him, and let Christian Gonzalez shadow Watson all day.

Paul: Gonzalez on Watson. That's the one I flew out here for.

Glen: You flew out here to tell strangers about your ledger.

Paul: Two birds.

Glen will be in his seat early, still talking about Gronk, still insisting the process matters more than the trophies. Paul will be a section away with his ledger in his coat pocket, ten days rested and twice as loud. Both of them know Gronk won his fourth ring in Tampa Bay, and neither of them wants to talk about it.

My call: Patriots 24, Packers 21.

Vic Moreno has one question for every game on the schedule, and he asked it before he set his bag down in Santa Clara: who's across the field? This week it's San Francisco, at Levi's Stadium, 4:25 p.m. Eastern on Fox, Kirk Cousins and Klint Kubiak against Brock Purdy and Kyle Shanahan. Nora Haskell found him Saturday after she'd spent the afternoon at CEFCU Stadium watching San Jose State and Northern Illinois. She was still in a teaching mood.

Nora: Count the rings, Vic. Five. The Catch started it. Montana to Dwight Clark, 58 seconds left, 1981 NFC title game. Bill Walsh went 10-4 in the playoffs.

Vic: Three in eight seasons. XI, XV, XVIII. Jim Otto, Art Shell and Ted Hendricks are in Canton. And nobody had to catch anything in the back of an end zone to get us started.

Nora: Our last ring was the 1994 season. I know. I count that one too. I count Super Bowl LIV against Kansas City, 31-20, every time somebody tells me an NFC title means something.

Vic: See, that's where we agree. Kansas City is the only name I put above yours.

That's the whole difference between them. Nora keeps score in rings and nothing else. Vic keeps score in grudges, and beating the right opponent in a lost season means more to him than beating a stranger in December. Sunday, both of them are getting what they want: a real opponent with a real record.

The Niners are 6-1, and nobody has won in their building yet, four tries and four losses. The 49ers have scored 197 points and allowed 139, and they sat home last weekend with their feet up. Las Vegas is 4-4, and the Raiders' split is the strangest in the building: 1-3 at home, 3-1 on the road. They went to New Jersey last Sunday and won 38-33.

Nora: You gave up 33 to the Jets.

Vic: And scored 38. Next question.

Nora: Your home record.

Vic: We play angry in other people's stadiums. Ask anybody who's hosted us.

Arizona Cardinals at Seattle Seahawks is Jacoby Brissett and Mike LaFleur against Sam Darnold and Mike Macdonald, 4:25 p.m. Eastern at Lumen Field. The weekend before it, Seattle is hosting the Seattle Sauna Festival at the National Nordic Museum in Ballard, and Kara Holm decided that was the right place to welcome a man from Arizona.

Neil Carver lasted about four minutes.

Neil: I live in a sauna from May to October. You people pay for this?

Kara: We pay for it in November. That's the point. You come in from the rain and you sweat out the week.

Neil: I've got a 3-5 team. The sweating comes free.

Kara has a Super Bowl title from February, and she won't let anybody, including herself, treat it like a permanent address. Seattle beat New England 29-13 in Super Bowl LX. Titles in XLVIII and LX. And her take on it never changes.

Kara: Champions get hunted. Every team on our schedule shows up like it's their Super Bowl. Chicago did it Monday night and beat us 34-17 in our own building. That's what the hunt looks like.

Neil: At least you had a hunt to lose. Show me the 2008 comparison. That team had an identity by now. This one is still introducing itself.

Neil measures every Cardinals team against the 2008 club that won the NFC, the franchise's only trip to a Super Bowl. The 1925 and 1947 titles are in the record book, and he'll tell you so, but he doesn't think anybody alive learned football from them.

Here's where the two of them actually stand. Seattle is 4-4, 3-2 at home, with 185 points scored and 159 allowed, and the Seahawks are back on the field six days after that Monday night loss. Arizona is 3-5, 0-3 at home and 3-2 on the road, and the Cardinals just won 33-30 in Dallas. They've given up 238 points in eight games, which is why Neil isn't smiling much.

Kara: You're better on the road than at home.

Neil: Feels that way. Maybe we should rent a stadium in Texas.

Neil's reasons to keep watching start with Trey McBride, a tight end who gets open against everybody and catches the ball when he's not. Budda Baker is still the heartbeat on defense, the kind of safety who hits you on first down and reminds you about it on fourth. Brissett started in Dallas, and Arizona also used Gardner Minshew at quarterback in that game. Neil wasn't going to pretend he knew more than that.

Kara's answer starts with two young guys who don't need an introduction in this city. Jaxon Smith-Njigba is Darnold's first read, second read and best argument. Devon Witherspoon plays corner like he's angry at the receiver's family. Macdonald's defense held New England to 13 in the biggest game of the year.

Neil: That was February. This is November.

Kara: I know exactly what month it is. The champs get chased in every one of them.

Neil: Then you know we're coming.

By the time they left Ballard, Neil had admitted the heat felt good, and Kara had admitted a team that keeps winning in other people's buildings is dangerous in hers. Sunday, the soccer crowd will be gone, the grass back to football, and the champs will be hunted again. Neil just wants his guys to be the ones doing the hunting for once.

My call: Seahawks 27, Cardinals 19.

Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Chicago Bears is Baker Mayfield and Todd Bowles against Caleb Williams and Ben Johnson, Sunday night at 8:20 Eastern from Soldier Field. Ringling Bros. is in Rosemont all weekend calling itself "The Greatest Show On Earth," and Walt Brenner would like a word with whoever wrote that sign.

Walt: The greatest show in this town was running before most of this league had a logo, and it doesn't need elephants.

Sal Ferris got in Sunday morning and Walt took him straight to the Chicago History Museum on North Clark, where the "Aquí en Chicago" exhibit was wrapping up with a closing program from noon to four. Walt figured a man from Tampa could stand to learn something about a city with real history.

Sal: You brought me to a museum on the day of a night game.

Walt: I brought you to the right building. We were here first. Red Grange. Bronko Nagurski. Eight championships between 1921 and 1963 before anybody had heard of a Super Bowl, and one more after it.

Sal: And you're going to tell me about 1985.

Walt: I'm going to tell you 1985 is one chapter. People who think it's the whole book never read the front of it.

Sal doesn't do nostalgia. Sal does accountability. When something goes wrong in Tampa, he wants a name, a decision and a bill, and this season he's got a strange one to file.

Sal: We're 3-5. We've scored 178 and allowed 151. We've outscored people and we're still two games in the hole. Who owns this? Bowles owns it. That's the job. You don't get to blame bounces when you've scored more than you've allowed.

Walt: That's a lot of words for 3-5.

Sal: The 178 and 151 are real. That's what makes me mad.

Here's what's real. Tampa Bay just shut out Atlanta 16-0, and the Buccaneers are 2-1 on the road and 1-4 at home. Chicago is 6-2, 3-1 at Soldier Field, with 214 points scored and 160 allowed, and the Bears are coming back on six days after going to Seattle on Monday night and winning 34-17.

Walt: Thirty-four in Seattle. On a Monday. Against the champs.

Sal: Your quarterback had a night. I'll give you that and nothing else.

Caleb Williams has Rome Odunze outside, Colston Loveland working the middle, and D'Andre Swift out of the backfield. Ben Johnson has given Williams a playbook with a little of everything in it, and Walt has stopped pretending he doesn't love it.

Sal's guys aren't impressed. Mayfield plays like every snap is a personal insult. Emeka Egbuka gets open fast, and Bucky Irving runs angry between the tackles. On defense, Vita Vea takes up two blockers and half the oxygen, and Antoine Winfield Jr. hits like he's being graded on it.

Sal: Lee Roy Selmon. Greatest Buccaneer. Our own Hall of Famer. Our defense still plays in his shadow and it should.

Walt: Nagurski played both ways.

Sal: Nagurski never had to deal with a Tampa August.

They walked out of the museum at four, and Walt pointed the car toward the lake. Sal asked him who owned it if the Bears lost at home on national television to a 3-5 team. Walt said nobody, because it wasn't going to happen, and that if it did, he'd blame the circus for stealing the crowd.

Sal: That's an excuse.

Walt: That's history. We were here first. We get to name the villain.

Sal said Tampa has two Super Bowls, XXXVII and LV, and nobody in Chicago has to remind him how many the Bears have since 1963. Walt said one, and that he'd like a second, and that Sunday night is a fine place to start building toward it.

My call: Bears 24, Buccaneers 20.

Buffalo Bills at Minnesota Vikings is Josh Allen and Joe Brady against Kyler Murray and Kevin O'Connell, Monday night at 8:15 Eastern on ESPN and ABC from U.S. Bank Stadium. Two teams at 6-1, a national audience, and two fans who refuse to get excited about any of it until the calendar flips to January.

Ellen Marsh flew in Saturday and Erik Dahl took her straight to Huntington Bank Stadium for Gophers and UCLA, an 11 a.m. kickoff on Salute to Service day. Erik wanted her to see what a Minnesota crowd sounds like in the cold. Ellen wanted to know when the real game was.

Ellen: Wake me in January.

Erik: It's November.

Ellen: Then I'm early.

Right before kickoff the student section did the ROW chant, oars in the air, and Ellen admitted it was louder than she expected. Erik said wait until Monday.

Ellen doesn't clap for division titles anymore. Buffalo has piled up enough of them that she treats them like utility bills. The last time the Bills finished a season as champions was 1965, the second of two straight AFL titles after 1964, and she has spent every year since asking out loud what it's going to take.

Erik is the same animal in a different jersey. Minnesota won the 1969 NFL championship and hasn't won a Super Bowl since. He gives credit for every fall win and saves his trust for January.

Erik: Seven games is a rumor. A longer one than five, but a rumor.

Ellen: Ours is a rumor with 233 points in it.

That's the Bills right now. They're 6-1, 3-0 on the road, with 233 points scored and 181 allowed, and they just beat Baltimore 36-10. Minnesota is also 6-1, 3-0 at home, with 140 scored and 93 allowed. The one loss came at Detroit, 19-15, and Erik has been chewing on it all week.

Erik: Ninety-three points in seven games. That's Brian Flores. That's a defense that shows up every week.

Ellen: It's a rumor, Erik.

Erik: It's a very well-coached rumor.

Ellen's case is the obvious one, and she makes it like she's bored of making it. Allen is the whole show. James Cook takes the hits so Allen doesn't have to, DJ Moore wins outside, and Dalton Kincaid finds the soft spot in the middle every time a defense leaves one.

Erik's answer has more names in it. Murray can hurt you with his arm or his legs. Justin Jefferson is still the guy every defensive coordinator plans around. T.J. Hockenson works the middle, and Aaron Jones still runs like a man ten years younger than he has any right to.

Ellen: Ten years younger is a strong claim.

Erik: I'll take it back. He runs young. That's all I'm saying.

Both teams had eight days to get ready. Both quarterbacks can turn a broken play into a highlight. And both of these fans have watched a great fall turn into a cold January more times than they want to count.

Monday, before kickoff, the Blind Boys of Alabama are doing "Songs in the Key of Life" at the Dakota on Nicollet Mall, a Gospel Music Hall of Fame group singing on a football night. Erik said if anybody can get a Vikings fan to hope out loud, it's them. Ellen said she'd hope in January, and only after the coin toss.

Erik: Seven games, Ellen.

Ellen: Wake me in January, Erik.

My call: Bills 24, Vikings 21.
